The first time I saw the ocean, I was five years old. My parents took me to a beach in Oregon, and the moment the waves crashed against the shore, I froze. The water was vast, endless, and terrifying in its beauty. I remember clutching my father’s hand, my small fingers disappearing into his rough palm, while the salt spray stung my cheeks. That day, I learned that the world was bigger than me—bigger than my fears, my doubts, my small, contained life.

Now, years later, I still feel that awe when I stand at the water’s edge. The ocean doesn’t care about my problems. It doesn’t care if I’m happy or sad, if I’ve succeeded or failed. It just *is*—wild, indifferent, and free. And in that indifference, there’s a strange kind of comfort. It reminds me that my life, too, is just a ripple in something much larger.

I’ve spent most of my life trying to control things—my career, my relationships, my future. But the ocean taught me that some things can’t be controlled. You can’t tame the waves. You can’t stop the tide. And maybe that’s okay. Maybe the point isn’t to control, but to flow.

Sometimes, when I’m overwhelmed, I close my eyes and imagine the sound of the waves. It’s a rhythm, a pulse, a reminder that life isn’t about holding on too tightly. It’s about letting go. Even if just for a moment. Even if just to the tide.
